sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! Scroll down directly below this slide to experiment with columnar Parquet projection, zone-map row group pruning, and bit-packed dictionary compression across varying schemas.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Lab 1, Kaito! Test how selecting a narrow feature slice of 25 columns out of 500 with 40% row-group survival slashes transferred I/O by 98%, while bit-packed dictionary encoding shrinks 10 million categorical strings by 21 times!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! Scroll down directly below this slide to explore small-file object-store latency breakdowns and simulate Optimistic Concurrency Control Compare-and-Swap commits under concurrent writers.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Lab 2, Kaito! Compare scanning 102,400 one-megabyte files against compacted 256-megabyte segments to observe a 43-fold speedup, then toggle OCC CAS mode to see how conflicting concurrent updates are cleanly aborted to protect ACID consistency!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1! A feature matrix contains 400 uniform columns totaling 800 megabytes. A training pipeline projects 20 feature columns and skips 75% of row groups via Parquet zone maps. How many megabytes are transferred compared to CSV, and what is the percentage reduction? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1, Kaito! Projecting 20 columns out of 400 retains 5% of columns. With 25% surviving row groups, calculate the total bytes transferred from 800 megabytes and find the reduction percentage.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding mathematical derivation! Selecting 20 out of 400 columns retains 5% of the schema. Multiplying by 25% surviving row groups yields an effective I/O ratio of 1.25%. That means only 10.0 megabytes are transferred from 800 megabytes, delivering a 98.75% I/O reduction and an 80-fold read speedup over CSV!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Review the projection and zone-map formula! Column projection ratio is 20 divided by 400, which is 0.05. Surviving row-group fraction is 1 minus 0.75, which is 0.25. Multiplying 0.05 by 0.25 gives 0.0125. Eight hundred megabytes times 0.0125 is 10.0 megabytes, an 80-fold reduction.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2! A 50-gigabyte partition arrives as 51,200 one-megabyte micro-files on S3. With 25-millisecond request overhead and 2.5 gigabytes per second bandwidth, what fraction of scan time is wasted waiting on metadata before compaction, and what speedup is achieved after compacting into 256-megabyte blocks? Select Option A, Option B, or Option C.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 2, Kaito! Multiplying 51,200 files by 25 milliseconds gives 1,280 seconds of HTTP GET latency, compared to 20 seconds of actual byte transfer. What fraction of time is wasted on metadata, and how fast is the compacted table?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot-on object-store performance analysis! Uncompacted scan spends 1,280 seconds waiting on metadata out of 1,300 seconds total, meaning 98.46% of query time is wasted on HTTP overhead! Compacting into 200 files of 256 megabytes slashes total scan time down to 25.0 seconds, achieving a 52.0-fold query acceleration!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Check your latency arithmetic! Uncompacted HTTP GET latency is 51,200 times 0.025 seconds, which is 1,280 seconds. Total latency is 1,280 plus 20 seconds of transfer, equaling 1,300 seconds. 1,280 divided by 1,300 is 98.46%. Compacted latency is 200 times 0.025 plus 20, which is 25 seconds, giving a 52-fold speedup.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 3! An ad-tech telemetry pipeline logs 8 million 20-byte categorical strings across 32 distinct symbols. Concurrently, Spark Job B reads files F5, F6, and F7 from Snapshot 20 for compaction while Job A commits Snapshot 21 deleting records from F7. Calculate dictionary footprint and determine Job B's CAS commit verdict.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Checkpoint 3! Thirty-two categories require 5 bits per row. And Job B read file F7, which Job A modified in Snapshot 21. Look at the options below and select the correct compression and OCC verdict.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Masterful Lakehouse architecture! Raw storage is 160 megabytes. Codeword width is 5 bits, so dictionary encoding consumes 640 bytes plus 5 megabytes, yielding 4.77 MiB and a 32-fold compression ratio! Meanwhile, Job B's read set intersects Job A's delete set at file F7, so the CAS commit aborts and rebases to prevent resurrecting deleted records!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Double-check your dictionary and OCC formulas! Log base 2 of 32 is 5 bits. Eight million times 5 bits divided by 8 is 5 million bytes, plus 640 dictionary bytes, totaling 4.77 MiB. Under Optimistic Concurrency Control, the read set contains F7 which was deleted in Snapshot 21, forcing an immediate abort and rebase.
